For the Prophet Ezekiel cried to the Jews,<div eID="gen135280" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen135281" type="x-p"/>“Walk ye not in the statutes of your fathers.”<lb/> (<reference osisRef="Bible:Ezek.20.18">Ezekiel 20:18</reference>.)<div eID="gen135281" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen135282" type="x-p"/>This ought also to be no less attended to by us in the present day; for, in order that the redemption of Christ may be effectual and useful to us, we must renounce our former life, though derived from the teaching and practice of our fathers. Thrice foolish, then, are the Papists, who think that the name of Fathers is a sufficient defense for all their superstitions, so that they boldly reject whatever is brought forward from the Word of God.<div eID="gen135282" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:1Pet.1.18" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen135274" osisID="1Pet.1.18" type="section"/>
entries.52ae7fe3407b9ddd7f235fc989d5444ad73762a0: <div annotateRef="Bible:1Pet.1.19" annotateType="commentary" osisID="1Pet.1.19" sID="gen135283" type="section"/> <div sID="gen135284" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">19</hi> <hi type="italic">As of a lamb</hi> He means by this similitude, that we have in Christ whatever had been shadowed forth by the ancient sacrifices, though he especially alludes to the Paschal lamb. But let us hence learn what benefit the reading of the Law brings us in this respect; for, though the rite of sacrificing is abolished, yet it assists our faith not a little, to compare the reality with the type, so that we may seek in the former what the latter contains. Moses ordered a whole or perfect lamb, without blemish, to be chosen for the Passover. The same thing is often repeated as to the sacrifices, as in <reference osisRef="Bible:Lev.23">Leviticus 23</reference>; in <reference osisRef="Bible:Num.28">Numbers 28</reference>; and in other places. Peter, by applying this to Christ, teaches us that he was a suitable victim, and approved by God, for he was perfect, without any blemish; had he had any defect in him, he could not have been rightly offered to God, nor could he pacify his wrath.<div eID="gen135284" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:1Pet.1.19" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen135283" osisID="1Pet.1.19" type="section"/>
entries.e9a4b24c1d601b544d9fbe28945100fee9338968: <div annotateRef="Bible:1Pet.1.20" annotateType="commentary" osisID="1Pet.1.20" sID="gen135285" type="section"/> <div sID="gen135286" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">20</hi> <hi type="italic">Who verily was foreordained</hi> He again by a comparison amplifies the grace of God, with which he had peculiarly favored the men of that age. For it was not a common or a small favor that God deferred the manifestation of Christ to that time, when yet he had ordained him in his eternal council for the salvation of the world. At the same time, however, he reminds us, that it was not a new or a sudden thing as to God that Christ appeared as a Savior; and this is what ought especially to be known. For, in addition to this, that novelty is always suspicious, what would be the stability of our faith, if we believed that a remedy for mankind had suddenly occurred at length to God after some thousands of years? In short, we cannot confidently recumb on Christ, except we are convinced that eternal salvation is in him, and always has been in him. Besides, Peter addressed the Jews, who had heard that he had already been long ago promised; and though they understood nothing true or clear or certain respecting his power and office, yet there remained among them a persuasion, that a Redeemer had been promised by God to the fathers.<div eID="gen135286" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen135287" type="x-p"/>It may yet be asked, As Adam did not fall before the creation of the world, how was it that Christ had been appointed the Redeemer? for a remedy is posterior to the disease. My reply is, that this is to be referred to God’s foreknowledge; for doubtless God, before he created man, foresaw that he would not stand long in his integrity. Hence he ordained, according to his wonderful wisdom and goodness, that Christ should be the Redeemer, to deliver the lost race of man from ruin. For herein shines forth more fully the unspeakable goodness of God, that he anticipated our disease by the remedy of his grace, and provided a restoration to life before the first man had fallen into death. If the reader wishes for more on this subject, he may find it in my Institutes.<div eID="gen135287" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen135288" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">But was manifest, </hi>or <hi type="italic">manifested</hi>. Included in these words, as I think, is not only the personal appearance of Christ, but also the proclamation of the Gospel. For, by the coming of Christ, God executed what he had decreed; and what he had obscurely indicated to the fathers is now clearly and plainly made known to us by the Gospel. He says that this was done <hi type="italic">in these last times, </hi>meaning the same as when Paul says,<div eID="gen135288" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen135289" type="x-p"/>“In the fullness of time,” (<reference osisRef="Bible:Gal.4.4">Galatians 4:4</reference>;)<div eID="gen135289" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen135290" type="x-p"/>for it was the mature season and the full time which God in his counsel had appointed.<div eID="gen135290" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen135291" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">For you</hi> He does not exclude the fathers, to whom the promise had not been useless; but as God has favored us more than them, he intimates that the greater the amplitude of grace towards us, the more reverence and ardor and care are required of us.<div eID="gen135291" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:1Pet.1.20" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen135285" osisID="1Pet.1.20" type="section"/>
entries.0d113c790f703edd1a4e5f17ee98f3369cfec3ad: <div annotateRef="Bible:1Pet.1.21" annotateType="commentary" osisID="1Pet.1.21" sID="gen135292" type="section"/> <div sID="gen135293" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">21</hi> <hi type="italic">Who believe</hi> The manifestation of Christ refers not to all indiscriminately, but belongs to those only on whom he by the Gospel shines. But we must notice the words, <hi type="italic">Who by him believe in God: </hi>here is shortly expressed what faith is. For, since God is incomprehensible, faith could never reach to him, except it had an immediate regard to Christ. Nay, there are two reasons why faith could not be in God, except Christ intervened as a Mediator: first, the greatness of the divine glory must be taken to the account, and at the same time the littleness of our capacity. Our acuteness is doubtless very far from being capable of ascending so high as to comprehend God. Hence all knowledge of God without Christ is a vast abyss which immediately swallows up all our thoughts. A clear proof of this we have, not only in the Turks and the Jews, who in the place of God worship their own dreams, but also in the Papists. Common is that axiom of the schools, that God is the object of faith. Thus of hidden majesty, Christ being overlooked, they largely and refinedly speculate; but with what success? They entangle themselves in astounding dotages, so that there is no end to their wanderings. For faith, as they think, is nothing else but an imaginative speculation. Let us, therefore, remember, that Christ is not in vain called <hi type="italic">the image of the invisible God</hi>, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Col.1.15">Colossians 1:15</reference>;) but this name is given to him for this reason, because God cannot be known except in him.<div eID="gen135293" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen135294" type="x-p"/>The second reason is, that as faith unites us to God, we shun and dread every access to him, except a Mediator comes who can deliver us from fear. For sin, which reigns in us, renders us hateful to God and him to us. Hence, as soon as mention is made of God, we must necessarily be filled with dread; and if we approach him, his justice is like fire, which will wholly consume us.<div eID="gen135294" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen135295" type="x-p"/>It is hence evident that we cannot believe in God except through Christ, in whom God in a manner makes himself little, that he might accommodate himself to our comprehension; and it is Christ alone who can tranquillize consciences, so that we may dare to come in confidence to God.<div eID="gen135295" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen135296" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">That raised him up from the dead</hi> He adds, that Christ had been raised up from the dead, in order that their faith and hope, by which they were supported, might have a firm foundation. And hereby again is confuted the gloss respecting universal and indiscriminate faith in God; for had there been no resurrection of Christ, still God would remain in heaven. But Peter says that he would not have been believed in, except Christ had risen. It is then evident, that faith is something else than to behold the naked majesty of God. And rightly does Peter speak in this manner; for it belongs to faith to penetrate into heaven, that it may find the Father there: how could it do so, except it had Christ as a leader?<div eID="gen135296" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen135297" type="x-p"/>“By him,” says Paul, “we have confidence of access.”<lb/> (<reference osisRef="Bible:Eph.3.12">Ephesians 3:12</reference>.)<div eID="gen135297" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen135298" type="x-p"/>It is said also, in <reference osisRef="Bible:Heb.4.16">Hebrews 4:16</reference>, that relying on our high priest, we can come with confidence to the throne of grace. Hope is the anchor of the soul, which enter into the inner part of the sanctuary; but not without Christ going before. (<reference osisRef="Bible:Heb.6.19">Hebrews 6:19</reference>.) Faith is our victory against the world, (<reference osisRef="Bible:1John.5.4">1 John 5:4</reference>) and what is it that makes it victorious, except that Christ, the Lord of heaven and earth, has us under his guardianship and protection?<div eID="gen135298" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen135299" type="x-p"/>As, then, our salvation depends on the resurrection of Christ and his supreme power, faith and hope find here what can support them. For, except he had by rising again triumphed over death, and held now the highest sovereignty, to protect us by his power, what would become of us, exposed to so great a power as that of our enemies, and to such violent attacks? Let us, therefore, learn to what mark we ought to direct our aim, so that we may really believe in God.<div eID="gen135299" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:1Pet.1.21" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen135292" osisID="1Pet.1.21" type="section"/>
entries.ed189738e52cbe661a497061b5ea387cd973e1bd:
22 Seeing ye have purified your souls, or, Purifying your souls. Erasmus badly renders the words, “Who have purified,” etc. For Peter does not declare what they had done, but reminds them of what they ought to do. The participle is indeed in the past tense, but it may be rendered as a gerund, “By purifying, etc.” The meaning is, that their souls would not be capable of receiving grace until they were purified, and by this our uncleanness is proved.
It is better to keep the tense of the participle, — “Having purified (or, since ye have purified) your souls by obeying the truth through the Spirit to an unfeigned love of the brethren, love ye one another fervently from a pure heart; having been born again,” etc.
The order here is similar to what is often found in Scripture; purification is mentioned before regeneration, as being the most visible and the effect; then what goes before it as being in a manner the cause. — Ed.
But that he might not seem to ascribe to us the power of purifying our souls, he immediately adds, through the Spirit; as though he had said, “Your souls are to be purified, but as ye cannot do this, offer them to God, that he may take away your filth by his Spirit.” He only mentions souls, though they needed to be cleansed also from the defilements of the flesh, as Paul bids the Corinthians, (2 Corinthians 7:1;) but as the principal uncleanness is within, and necessarily draws with it that which is outward, Peter was satisfied with mentioning only the former, as though he had said, that not outward actions only ought to be corrected, but the very hearts ought to be thoroughly reformed.
He afterwards points out the manner, for purity of soul consists in obedience to God. Truth is to be taken for the rule which God prescribes to us in the Gospel. Nor does he speak only of works, but rather faith holds here the primacy. Hence Paul specially teaches us in the first and last chapter of the Epistle to the Romans, that faith is that by which we obey God; and Peter in Acts, the fifteenth chapter, bestows on it this eulogy, that God by it purifies the heart.
Unto love of the brethren, or, Unto brotherly love. He briefly reminds us what God especially requires in our life, and the mark to which all our endeavors should be directed. So Paul in the first chapter of the Epistle to the Ephesians, when speaking of the perfection of the faithful, makes it to consist in love. And this is what we ought the more carefully to notice, because the world makes its own sanctity to consist of the veriest trifles, and almost overlooks this the chief thing. We see how the Papists weary themselves beyond measure with thousand invented superstitions: in the meantime, the last thing is that love which God especially commends. This, then, is the reason why Peter calls our attention to it, when speaking of a life rightly formed.
He had before spoken of the mortification of the flesh, and of our conformity with the will of God; but he now reminds us of what God would have us to cultivate through life, that is, mutual love towards one another; for by that we testify also that we love God; and by this evidence God proves who they are who really love him.
He calls it unfeigned, (ἀνυπόκριτον), as Paul calls faith in 1 Timothy 1:5; for nothing is more difficult than to love our neighbors in sincerity. For the love of ourselves rules, which is full of hypocrisy; and besides, every one measures his love, which he shews to others, by his own advantage, and not by the rule of doing good. He adds, fervently; for the more slothful we are by nature, the more ought every one to stimulate himself to fervor and earnestness, and that not only once, but more and more daily.
1 Peter 1:23-25
23. Being born again, not of corruptible seed, but of incorruptible, by the word of God, which liveth and abideth for ever.
23. Regeniti non ex semine corruptibili, sed incorruptibili, per sermonem viventis Dei et manentis in aeternum.
24. For all flesh is as grass, and all the glory of man as the flower of grass. The grass withereth, and the flower thereof falleth away:
24. Quandoquidem omnis caro tanquam herba, et omnis gloria ejus tanquam flos herbae; exaruit herba et flos ejus decidit:
25. But the word of the Lord endureth for ever. And this is the word which by the gospel is preached unto you.
25. Verbum autem Domini manet in aeternum; hoc autem est verbum quod annuntiatum est vobis.
entries.40873e4ead2b45d9a5300b31281115b0d92c4132: <div annotateRef="Bible:1Pet.1.23" annotateType="commentary" osisID="1Pet.1.23" sID="gen135317" type="section"/> <div sID="gen135318" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">23</hi> <hi type="italic">Being born again</hi> Here is another reason for an exhortation, — that since they were new men and born again of God, it behoved them to form a life worthy of God and of their spiritual regeneration. And this seems to be connected with a verse in <reference osisRef="Bible:1Pet.2.2">the next chapter</reference> respecting the milk of the word, which they were to seek, that their way of living might correspond with their birth. It may, however, be extended wider, so as to be connected also with what has gone before; for Peter collected together those things which may lead us to an upright and a holy life. The object, then, of Peter was to teach us that we cannot be Christians without regeneration; for the Gospel is not preached, that it may be only heard by us, but that it may, as a seed of immortal life, altogether reform our hearts. <note n="18"> <div sID="gen135319" type="x-p"/> Most commentators, like <hi type="italic">Calvin, </hi>represent the <hi type="italic">seed </hi>as the word; but the construction does not admit this; the words are, “Having been begotten from a seed, not corruptible, but incorruptible, through the living word of God, and for-ever abiding.” The “seed” denotes evidently the vital principle of grace, the new nature, the restored image of God; it is the same with what John means when he says,<div eID="gen135319" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen135320" type="x-p"/>“His seed (that is, of God) remaineth in him.” (<reference osisRef="Bible:1John.3.9">1 John 3:9</reference>.)<div eID="gen135320" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen135321" type="x-p"/>Then “the word” is set forth as the means or instrument by which this seed is implanted. The “living” here does not mean life-giving, as some interpret it, but stands opposed to what ceases to be valid: and “for-ever abiding” more fully expresses its meaning. The metaphor in the parable of the sower is quite different: the word there is compared to a seed sown on bad or good ground; but here the turning of a bad into a good ground is the subject; and in this process the word is employed as an instrument. — <hi type="italic">Ed.</hi><div eID="gen135321" type="x-p"/> </note> Moreover, the <hi type="italic">corruptible seed</hi> is set in opposition to God’s word, in order that the faithful might know that they ought to renounce their former nature, and that it might be more evident how much is the difference between the children of Adam who are born only into the world, and the children of God who are renewed into a heavenly life. But as the construction of the Greek text is doubtful, we may read, “the living word of God,” as well as, “the word of the living God.” As, however, the latter reading is less forced, I prefer it; though it must be observed, that the term is applied to God owing to the character of the passage. For, as in <reference osisRef="Bible:Heb.4.12">Hebrews 4:12</reference>, because God sees all things, and nothing is hid from him, the apostle argues that the word of God penetrates into the inmost marrow, so as to discern thoughts and feelings; so, when Peter in this place calls him the living God, who abides for ever, he refers to the word, in which the perpetuity of God shines forth as in a living mirror.<div eID="gen135318" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:1Pet.1.23" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen135317" osisID="1Pet.1.23" type="section"/>
entries.5eeac2f5310c0022c8375bb58954ef49f9256d55: <div annotateRef="Bible:1Pet.1.24" annotateType="commentary" osisID="1Pet.1.24" sID="gen135322" type="section"/> <div sID="gen135323" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">24</hi> <hi type="italic">For all flesh</hi> He aptly quotes the passage from Isaiah to prove both clauses; that is, to make it evident how fading and miserable is the first birth of man, and how great is the grace of the new birth. For as the Prophet there speaks of the restoration of the Church, to prepare the way for it, he reduces men to nothing lest they should flatter themselves. I know that the words are wrongly turned by some to another sense; for some explain them of the Assyrians, as though the Prophet said, that there was no reason for the Jews to fear so much from flesh, which is like a fading flower. Others think that the vain confidence which the Jews reposed in human aids, is reproved. But the Prophet himself disproves both these views, by adding, that the people were as grass; for he expressly condemns the Jews for vanity, to whom he promised restoration in the name of the Lord. This, then, is what I have already said, that until their own emptiness has been shewn to men, they are not prepared to receive the grace of God. In short, such is the meaning of the Prophet: as exile was to the Jews like death, he promised them a new consolation, even that God would send prophets with a command of this kind. The Lord, he says, will yet say, “Comfort ye my people;” and that in the desert and the waste, the prophetic voice would yet be heard, in order that a way might be prepared for the Lord. (<reference osisRef="Bible:Isa.40.6">Isaiah 40:6</reference>.)<div eID="gen135323" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen135324" type="x-p"/>And as the obstinate pride which filled them, must have been necessarily purged from their minds, in order that an access might be open for God, the Prophet added what Peter relates here respecting the vanishing glory of the flesh. What is man? he says — <hi type="italic">grass</hi>; what is the glory of man? <hi type="italic">the flower of the grass</hi>. For as it was difficult to believe that man, in whom so much excellency appears, is like grass, the Prophet made a kind of concession, as though he had said, “Be it, indeed, that flesh has some glory; but lest that should dazzle your eyes, know that the flower soon withers.” He afterwards shews how suddenly everything that seems beautiful in men vanishes, even through the blowing of the Spirit of God; and by this he intimates, that man seems to be something until he comes to God, but that his whole brightness is as nothing in his presence; that, in a word, his glory is in this world, and has no place in the heavenly kingdom.<div eID="gen135324" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen135325" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">The grass withereth, </hi>or, <hi type="italic">has withered</hi>. Many think that this refers only to the outward man; but they are mistaken; for we must consider the comparison between God’s word and man. For if he meant only the body and what belongs to the present life, he ought to have said, in the second place, that the soul was far more excellent. But what he sets in opposition to the grass and its flower, is the word of God. It then follows, that in man nothing but vanity is found. Therefore, when Isaiah spoke of flesh and its glory, he meant the whole man, such as he is in himself; for what he ascribed as peculiar to God’s word, he denied to man. In short, the Prophet speaks of the same thing as Christ does in <reference osisRef="Bible:John.3.3">John 3:3</reference>, that man is wholly alienated from the kingdom of God, that he is nothing but an earthly, fading, and empty creature, until he is born again.<div eID="gen135325" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:1Pet.1.24" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen135322" osisID="1Pet.1.24" type="section"/>
entries.1791ee67eddf74f65e5262deed592e32965a0541:
25 But the word of God The Prophet does not shew what the word of God is in itself, but what we ought to think of it; for since man is vanity in himself, it remains that he ought to seek life elsewhere. Hence Peter ascribes power and efficacy to God’s word, according to the authority of the Prophet, so that it can confer on us what is real, solid, and eternal. For this was what the Prophet had in view, that there is no permanent life but in God, and that this is communicated to us by the word. However fading, then, is the nature of man, yet he is made eternal by the word; for he is re-moulded and becomes a new creature.
This is the word which by the gospel is preached unto you, or, which has been declared to you. He first reminds us, that when the word of God is mentioned, we are very foolish if we imagine it to be remote from us in the air or in heaven; for we ought to know that it has been revealed to us by the Lord. What, then, is this word of the Lord, which gives us life? Even the Law, the Prophets, the Gospel. Those who wander beyond these limits of revelation, find nothing but the impostures of Satan and his dotages, and not the word of the Lord. We ought the more carefully to notice this, because impious and Luciferian men, craftily allowing to God’s word its own honor, at the same time attempt to draw us away from the Scriptures, as that unprincipled man, Agrippa, who highly extols the eternity of God’s word, and yet treats with scurrility the Prophets, and thus indirectly laughs to scorn the Word of God.
In short, as I have already reminded you, no mention is here made of the word which lies hid in the bosom of God, but of that which has proceeded from his mouth, and has come to us. So again it ought to be borne in mind, that God designed by the Apostles and Prophets to speak to us, and their mouths is the mouth of the only true God.
Then, when Peter says, Which has been announced, or declared, to you, he intimates that the word is not to be sought elsewhere than in the Gospel preached to us; and truly we know not the way of eternal life otherwise than by faith. But there can be no faith, except we know that the word is destined for us.
To the same purpose is what Moses said to the people,
“Say not in thine heart, Who shall ascend into heaven, etc.; nigh is the word, in thy mouth and in thy heart.” (Deuteronomy 30:12.)
That these words agree with what Peter says, Paul shews Romans 10:6, where he teaches us that it was the word of faith which he preached.
There is here, besides, no common eulogy on preaching; for Peter declares that what is preached is the life-giving word. God alone is indeed he who regenerates us; but for that purpose he employs the ministry of men; and on this account Paul glories that the Corinthians had been spiritually begotten by him. (1 Corinthians 4:15.) It is indeed certain that those who plant and those who water, are nothing; but whenever God is pleased to bless their labor, he makes their doctrine efficacious by the power of his Spirit; and the voice which is in itself mortal, is made an instrument to communicate eternal life.
CHAPTER 2
1 Peter 2:1-5
1. Wherefore laying aside all malice, and all guile, and hypocrisies, and envies, and all evil speakings,
1. Proinde deposita omni malitia et omni dolo et simulationibus et invidiis et omnibus obtrectationibus,
2. As newborn babes, desire the sincere milk of the word, that ye may grow thereby:
2. Tanquam modò geniti infantes, lac rationale et dolo vacuum appetite, ut per illud subolescatis:
3. If so be ye have tasted that the Lord is gracious.
3. Si quidem gustastis quòd benignus sit Dominus;
4. To whom coming, as unto a living stone, disallowed indeed of men, but chosen of God, and precious,
4. Ad quem accedentes, qui est lapis vivus, ab hominibus quidera reprobatus, apud Deum vero electus ac pretiosus;
5. Ye also, as lively stones, are built up a spiritual house, an holy priesthood, to offer up spiritual sacrifices, acceptable to God by Jesus Christ.
5. Ipsi quoque tanquam vivi lapides, aedificamini, domus spirituales, sacerdotium sanctum, ad offerendas spirituales hostias, acceptas Deo per Jesum Christum.

These several words shew whither pre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sent Trials tend, and in what they issue; they may be re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />proachful and ignominious now (<ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 12.2.) but they end in Glory. We need not be critical about the difference of these three words, <ns0:hi>Praise, Honour,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Glory,</ns0:hi> which may be synonimous Expressions (by way of Amplification) of the same thing, yet they are mentioned distinctly with relation to Believers elsewhere, <ns0:hi>Praise,</ns0:hi> 1 Cor. 4.5. <ns0:hi>Honour,</ns0:hi> 1 Sam. 2.30. <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> 12.26. <ns0:hi>Glory</ns0:hi> as well as Honour, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 2.10.</ns0:note>, at the appearing <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">i. e. At the Day of Judgment frequently so called, as <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 13. and <ns0:hi>Colos.</ns0:hi> 3.4. 2 <ns0:hi>Thess.</ns0:hi> 1.7. and <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 5.4. Christ's Glory is at present hid and obscured, while he is instructing his Elect, and training them up unto Patience, and defers his judging of his Enemies; but at last it will be fully manifested in the Face of the World, when <ns0:hi>he comes with Clouds, and every Eye shall see him,</ns0:hi> &c. Rev. 1.7.</ns0:note> of Jesus Christ.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="8">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:580" />8 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 Joh. 4.20.</ns0:note> Whom <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">Which Christ.</ns0:note> having not seen <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">With your bodily Eyes. Most of these <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> lived out of their own Country, and so had not seen Christ in the Flesh; and this was the Commendation of their Love, that they loved him whom they had not seen, though sight doth ordinarily contribute toward the stirring up of Af<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fection.</ns0:note>, ye love <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Joh. 20.29. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>eb. 11.1, 27.</ns0:note>, in whom though now ye see <ns0:hi>him</ns0:hi> not <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">Neither as others have done in the daies of his Flesh, nor as you your selves hereafter shall in his Glory; ye <ns0:hi>walk by Faith, and not by sight,</ns0:hi> 2 Cor. 5.7.</ns0:note>, yet be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lieving, ye rejoice <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">In hope of seeing and enjoying him.</ns0:note> with joy unspeakable <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Which cannot be expressed with Words. See the like Phrase, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 8.26. and 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 9.15.</ns0:note>, and full of glory <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Both in respect of the Object about which this Joy is conversant, the heavenly Glory; the Degree, it is the high<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />est here in the World, the duration of it, it is most solid; as likewise in Comparison of the Joy of this World which is vain and transitory, and whereof many times Men are af<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />terward ashamed.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="9">9 Receiving <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Either this word is to be taken improperly, and by an Enallage, the Future being put for the Present Tense, <ns0:hi>q. d.</ns0:hi> being about to receive; or rather properly in the Present Tense, and then it intimates the certainty of the thing spoken of.</ns0:note> the end <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">i. e. The Scope to which Faith tends, or the Reward of Faith.</ns0:note> of your faith, <ns0:hi>even</ns0:hi> the salvation <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Either, 1. Salvation more generally taken, which is begun in this Life, <ns0:hi>Ephes.</ns0:hi> 2.8. <ns0:hi>Tit.</ns0:hi> 3.5. or rather, 2. com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />plete final Salvation in the other, as <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 5. and then the Sense is, either ye rejoice that ye shall certainly receive the full Salvation of your Souls, or ye rejoice that ye do receive that Salvation, <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> in the Promises of it, in those Graces of the Spirit wrought in you, which begin this Salvation, and are the Pledges of it, and in the certain Assurance of it.</ns0:note> of <ns0:hi>your</ns0:hi> souls <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">i. e. (By an usual Synechdoche) the Salvation of your persons.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="10">10 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Gen. 49.10. Dan. 2.44. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>ag. 2.8. Zech. 6.12. Mat. 13.17.</ns0:note> Of which salvation <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Either, 1. the more full and clear Manifestation of Sal<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vation promised to be at the coming of Christ, when <ns0:hi>Life and Immortality</ns0:hi> should be <ns0:hi>brought to light through the Gospel,</ns0:hi> 2 Tim. 1.10. and then this place is parallel to <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> 10.24. Or, 2. the Salvation of the dispersed <ns0:hi>Iews,</ns0:hi> i. e. their publick Conversion by the Gospel, and eternal Life following upon it; which (as well as the Calling of the Gentiles) was reser<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ved for the Times and Glory of the <ns0:hi>Messiah.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> the Prophets <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Viz.</ns0:hi> Those under the Old-Testament, out of whose Writings the Faith of New-Testament-Believers is to be confirmed, <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> 5.39. <ns0:hi>Acts</ns0:hi> 17.11. and whom this Apostle therefore mentions, that he might strengthen the Faith of the Christian <ns0:hi>Iews,</ns0:hi> by assuring them that the Doctrine he had delivered to them, was no new Invention, but the very Truth of God revealed of old to the Prophets.</ns0:note> have enquired, and searched diligently <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">The words imply their vehement de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sire of knowing, as well as great diligence in seeking.</ns0:note>, who pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />phesied of the grace <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">What he called <ns0:hi>Salvation</ns0:hi> before, he calls <ns0:hi>Grace</ns0:hi> here, to intimate their Salvation to be meerly of Grace. This Grace revealed under the Gospel, the Prophets foretold, but in a more dark way; the Sun of Righteousness not being yet risen, the Sha<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dows were not gone, and the Light was but obscure.</ns0:note> 
                  <ns0:hi>that should come</ns0:hi> unto you.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="11">11 Searching what <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Whether near or further off, or what particular part of time. This may relate particularly to <ns0:hi>Daniel</ns0:hi>'s Weeks, <ns0:hi>ch.</ns0:hi> 9.</ns0:note>, or what manner of time <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Whether peaceable or troublesom, when the Peo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ple were free, or when in Bondage; what were the Qualities of the time, or Signs by which it might be known. <ns0:hi>Iacob</ns0:hi> fore-tells Christ's coming, when the Scepter was departed from <ns0:hi>Iudah, Gen.</ns0:hi> 49.10. <ns0:hi>Isaiah,</ns0:hi> in a time of Universal Peace, <ns0:hi>ch.</ns0:hi> 2.4. and 11.6. This diligent enquiring after the time of Christ's coming, shewed their earnest longing for it.</ns0:note> the <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">2 Pet. 1.21.</ns0:note> spirit of Christ <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">So stiled, as being of the Son, no less than of the Father, both by eternal Procession, and temporal Mission, <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> 14.16, 26. & 15.26. This shews, that not only Christ had a Being under the Old Testament before his coming in the Flesh, (for if Christ were not, there could be no Spirit of Christ) and likewise that Christ is God, because of his inspiring the Prophets with the Knowledge of future things, which none but God can do.</ns0:note> which was in them did signifie, when it <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">What the Prophets did foretel concerning Christ, was not their own Conjecture, but what the Spirit did dictate to them.</ns0:note> testified before-hand the sufferings of Christ, and the glory <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Gr. <ns0:hi>Glories,</ns0:hi> in the Plural Number, <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> the manifold Glory which was to follow upon his many Sufferings, the Glory of his Resurrection, Ascension, sitting at the Right-Hand of God, sending the Spirit, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> Christ's Sufferings and Glory are of<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ten joined together, <ns0:hi>Psalm</ns0:hi> 22.6. and 110. <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 53.3, 10, 11, 12. <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> 24.26. <ns0:hi>Phil.</ns0:hi> 2.8, 9. <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 2.9, 10. to shew that there is the same way (and no other) for the Salvation of the Members, as for the Glory of the Head, <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> by Sufferings.</ns0:note> that should follow.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="12">12 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Dan. 9.24. and 12.9, 13.</ns0:note> Unto whom <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Unto which Prophets.</ns0:note> it was revealed <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Viz.</ns0:hi> by the Spirit of Christ that was in them,</ns0:note>, that not unto themselves <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">who lived before Christ's coming in the Flesh.</ns0:note>, but unto us <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">Not only Apostles, but Believers, who live since Christ came.</ns0:note> they did mi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nister <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">Declare and foretel. The preaching of the Word is called a Ministry, <ns0:hi>Acts</ns0:hi> 6.4. and 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 4.1. and 5.18.</ns0:note> the things <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">The whole Doctrine of the Gospel concerning Christ's Person, Offices, Benefits, Kingdom, and the whole New Testament-state.</ns0:note> which are now reported <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Viz.</ns0:hi> as fulfilled, and actually exhibited now, which were only foretold by the Prophets.</ns0:note> unto you by them <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">The Apostles and other Gospel-Ministers assistant to them: the sense is, The Prophets under the Old Testament did, by the Spirit, foresee, and foretel Christ's Passion, Resurrection, Ascension, the Effusion of the Spirit, the Enlargement of the Church, by the Calling of the Gentiles<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> 
                     <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> but did not live to see their own Prophecies, and God's Promises fulfilled, <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 11.13. as you now do. They did spread the Table that you might feed at it; they had but a taste by Faith, and at a distance, of those things you feast upon in their Ac<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />complishment; yet they did not grudge to declare these things, being instructed by the Spirit, that what they spake of, should not be fulfilled in their time, but in the Genera<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tions to come; that so ye<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> by comparing what they said should come to pass, with what you have now been as<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sured is come to pass, may be confirmed and established in the Belief of the Truth, beeing the same held forth by the Prophets formerly, and Gospel-Ministers at present:</ns0:note> that have preached the gospel unto you, with the <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Acts 2.4.</ns0:note> holy Ghost sent down from heaven <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Christ promised to send the Spirit, <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> 24.49. <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> 14.26. and 15.26. and 16.7. and actually sent him, <ns0:hi>Acts</ns0:hi> 2. the Apo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stles, not of themselves, but acted by this Spirit, have de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />clared unto you the fulfilling of those things, which the for<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mer Prophets, by the instinct and Power of the same Spirit (the Spirit of Christ, which was in them) did foretel, would in their proper season come to pass.</ns0:note>, which things <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">The things before-said to be reported by them that preached the Go<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />spel.</ns0:note> the angels desire to look into <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">It seems to be an Allusion to the Cherubims that stood above the Ark, with their Faces toward the Mer<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cy-seat, which was a Type of Christ. The word signifies a bowing down the Head, and stooping to look into a thing, <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> 24.12. <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> 20.5. and implies a prying, or look<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing narrowly into it; which argues an earnest desire to know it. The Angels thus look into the Mysteries of the Gospel, as desirous to see the Accomplishment of them, admiring the manifold Grace and Wisdom of God in them, <ns0:hi>Eph.</ns0:hi> 3.10. and rejoicing in the Salvation of Sinners, which is the end, and effect of God's revealing them.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="13">13 Wherefore <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">The following Exhortation may be connected, either with <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 4. being so glorious an Inheritance is reserved in Heaven for you, <ns0:hi>gird up,</ns0:hi> &c. or with <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 12. seeing ye know those things, which the Prophets that foretold them, did not fully see, and the Angels themselves desire to look into; the Grace of God vouchsafed to you, is so excellent and ad<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mirable, <ns0:hi>gird up,</ns0:hi> &c.</ns0:note> 
                  <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Eph. 6.14.</ns0:note> gird up the loins of your mind <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Let your Minds be attent, prompt, ready, prepared for your spiritual Work, restrain<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed from all those Thoughts, Cares, Affections, and Lusts, which may entangle, detain, hinder them, or make them unfit for it. It is a Metaphor taken from the Custom of the Oriental Nations, who wearing long loose Garments, were wont to gird them up about their Loins, that they might not hinder them in their travelling, or working, 1 <ns0:hi>King.</ns0:hi> 18.46. and 2 <ns0:hi>King.</ns0:hi> 4.29. <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> 17.8. See on <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> 12.35, 37. Perhaps it may have a special Respect to the like Rite used at the Passover, <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 12.11. when the <ns0:hi>Israelites</ns0:hi> were just ready to enter upon their Journey, and go out of <ns0:hi>Egypt.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>, be sober <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">This may relate, either, 1. to the Body, and then the sense agrees with <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> 21.34. where <ns0:hi>the Cares of this Life</ns0:hi> seem to be opposed to the girding up the Loins of the Mind, and <ns0:hi>Surfeiting and Drunkenness,</ns0:hi> to Sobriety here. Or rather, 2. to the Soul, and then girding up the Loins of the Mind, may refer to the Understanding, and Thoughts, and Sobrie<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ty, to the VVill and Affections, and may signifie that Mode<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ration which belongs to them, in Opposition to their Inor<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dinateness, which is a sort of Drunkenness. Or, it may be rendred, be <ns0:hi>watchful,</ns0:hi> as it is translated, 2 <ns0:hi>Tim.</ns0:hi> 4.5. and with which it is joined, 1 <ns0:hi>Thess.</ns0:hi> 5.6, 8. and so it agrees well with the former clause; they that have the Loins of their Mind girt up, being of a vigilant, present Mind, and ready for any VVork, they are to undertake.</ns0:note>, and hope <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>perfectly.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> to the end <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Gr. <ns0:hi>perfectly,</ns0:hi> as in the Mar<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gin, <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> sincerely, entirely, with a firm Confidence; but the following words favour our Translation, which signifies Perse<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />verance in hope. See <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 3.6.</ns0:note> for the grace <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Final Salvation, which is the Gift of Grace, <ns0:hi>Rom,</ns0:hi> 6.23. and is called the Grace of Life, 1 <ns0:hi>Pet.</ns0:hi> 3.7.</ns0:note>, that is to be brought unto you at the revelation <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Called the appearing of Jesus Christ, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 7.</ns0:note> of Jesus Christ.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="14">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:581" />14 As obedient children <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Gr. <ns0:hi>Children of Obedience,</ns0:hi> by an usual Hebraism for obedient Children. So <ns0:hi>Children of Disobedience,</ns0:hi> Eph. 2.2. <ns0:hi>Col.</ns0:hi> 3.6. and this we may understand either absolutely, Children of obedience for obedient Persons; or with relation to God, obedient Children of God; and then the Apostle perswades them to their Duty by an Argument taken from their Adoption; being the Chil<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dren of God, he would have them behave themselves obe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />diently, as becomes them in that Relation.</ns0:note>, not fashioning <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Not accommo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dating, not conforming your selves, not shaping, or ordering your Conversation. See the same word, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 12.2.</ns0:note> your selves according to the former lusts <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">The Lusts you formerly indulged your selves in. See <ns0:hi>Ephes.</ns0:hi> 4.22.</ns0:note>, in your ignorance <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Your Ignorance of Christ and the Gospel, <ns0:hi>q. d.</ns0:hi> not fashion<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing your selves according to those Lusts you lived in, when you were ignorant of Christ. He distinguisheth between the time of their Ignorance, and of their Illumination. A<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nother Age requires other manners. They formerly lived according to the Dictates of their Lusts, but now ought to live according to the VVill of Christ. See <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 18. <ns0:hi>Acts</ns0:hi> 17.30. <ns0:hi>Ephes.</ns0:hi> 4.17, 18.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="15">15 But as he <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">God the Father, to whom, as the first Cause, our Cal<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ling is frequently ascribed, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 9.11, 24. and 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 7.15. <ns0:hi>Gal.</ns0:hi> 1.6, 15. It may be rendred, <ns0:hi>according to the holy One that hath called you,</ns0:hi> i. e. according to his Example; you are Children, and should therefore imitate your Father, <ns0:hi>Ephes.</ns0:hi> 5.1.</ns0:note> that hath called <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> Effectually, to the Knowledg and Faith of Christ.</ns0:note> you, is holy <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">So God is often stiled by <ns0:hi>Isaiah,</ns0:hi> and other Pen-men of the Scripture, as the Fountain and Exemplar of Holiness.</ns0:note>, so be ye holy in all manner of con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />versation <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">Either through the whole Course, and in the several parts of your Conversation, or <ns0:hi>in all manner of Con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />versation,</ns0:hi> as we read it, <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> with whomsoever ye converse, Believers or Infidels, Friends or Enemies, Relations or Strangers; and in whatsoever Condition ye are in, Peace or Trouble, Prosperity or Adversity.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="16">16 Because it is written, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Lev. 11.44. and 19.2. and 20.7.</ns0:note> Be ye holy, for I <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">I your Father, and therefore you ought to imitate, and obey me: Or, I that have severed you from other People, that you should be mine, <ns0:hi>Lev.</ns0:hi> 20.26. to which place par<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ticularly this seems to refer.</ns0:note> am holy.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="17">17 And if <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">This Particle is used here, and frequently elsewhere, not as a Note of doubting, but by way of Assertion, and supposition of a thing known.</ns0:note> ye call on <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">Either this is to be meant of Invocation, their calling on God in Prayer; and then the sense is, If you be Servants, and Worshippers of the Father: Prayer being many times put for the whole Worship of God, <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 43.22. <ns0:hi>Acts</ns0:hi> 9.11. or of their calling God, Father, as <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 6.9. and then the sense is, If you would be count<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed God's Children, <ns0:hi>Iames</ns0:hi> 2.7.</ns0:note> the father, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Deut. 10.17. Rom. 2.11.</ns0:note> who, without respect of persons <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">And so will no more ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cuse you that are <ns0:hi>Iews,</ns0:hi> and descended from <ns0:hi>Abraham,</ns0:hi> than those that are born of Gentile Parents, <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> 34.19. <ns0:hi>Acts</ns0:hi> 10.34. <ns0:hi>Ephes.</ns0:hi> 6.9.</ns0:note>, judgeth <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">And so is not a Father only, but a Judge, and that a most righteous one.</ns0:note> accord<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing to every mans work <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>i. e. Works,</ns0:hi> the Singular Number put<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> for the Plural, as <ns0:hi>Iames</ns0:hi> 1.25. See <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 2.6. <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> 34.11.</ns0:note>: <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">2 Cor. 7.1.</ns0:note> pass the time of your sojourning <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">The word signifies the temporary abode of a Man in a place where he was not born, or doth not or<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dinarily reside; such being the Condition of Believers in the World, that they are Sojourners, not Citizens of it; they are travelling through it to their Father's House, and heaven<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly Country, <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 11.9, 10, 13, 16. They are here exhorted to a sutable Carriage expressed in the next words,</ns0:note> here in fear <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">VVhich is due to him as a Father, and a Judge.
